## Introduction

```{r, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(rfm)
library(dplyr)
library(rlang)
library(scales)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(magrittr)
library(ggplot2)
library(DT)
library(grDevices)
library(RColorBrewer)
options(knitr.table.format = "html")
```

This article provides a brief introduction to RFM analysis and customer segmentation. It scores the bundled orders, labels customers with a recommended six-segment scheme, and keeps the classic ten segments as a second example.

**RFM** (recency, frequency, monetary) analysis is a behaviour-based technique used to segment customers by examining their transaction history such as

- how recently a customer has purchased (recency)
- how often they purchase (frequency)
- how much the customer spends (monetary)

It is based on the marketing axiom that **80% of your business comes from 20% of your customers**. RFM helps to identify customers who are more likely to respond to promotions by segmenting them into various categories.

## Data

To calculate the RFM score for each customer we need data for a particular time frame and should include the following:

- a unique customer id 
- date of transaction/order
- transaction/order amount

Data can be at customer level or transaction level i.e. each row in the data may represent a single transaction of a customer or summary of all transactions of a customer. `rfm` package includes two sample data sets:

- `rfm_data_orders`

```{r rfm_data_orders}
head(rfm_data_orders)
```

- `rfm_data_customer`

```{r rfm_data_customer}
head(rfm_data_customer)
```

You can take a look at them to understand the difference between customer and transaction level data. **Remember, the data sets are different and the final results will not match.**

## RFM Score

Automatic bins use right-closed quantile intervals: values equal to a cut point
stay in the lower interval, including ties. The first interval includes the
minimum. Recency scores decrease as days increase; frequency and monetary
scores increase with their values. Custom thresholds remain lower-inclusive.
Since 0.5.1, automatic cut points no longer add one, making monetary scores
independent of currency units; customers near a cut point may change score or
segment.

So how is the RFM score computed for each customer? The below steps explain the process:

- A recency score is assigned to each customer based on date of most recent purchase. The score is generated by binning the recency values into a number of categories (default is 5). For example, if you use four categories, the customers with the most recent purchase dates receive a recency ranking of 4, and those with purchase dates in the distant past receive a recency ranking of 1.

- A frequency ranking is assigned in a similar way. Customers with high purchase frequency are assigned a higher score (4 or 5) and those with lowest frequency are assigned a score 1.

- Monetary score is assigned on the basis of the total revenue generated by the customer in the period under consideration for the analysis. Customers with highest revenue/order amount are assigned a higher score while those with lowest revenue are assigned a score of 1.

- A fourth score, RFM score is generated which is simply the three individual scores concatenated into a single value.

The customers with the highest RFM scores are most likely to respond to an offer. Now that we have understood how the RFM score is computed, it is time to put it into practice. Use `rfm_table_order()` to generate the score for each customer from the sample data set `rfm_data_orders`.

```{r rfm_table_order, eval=FALSE}
analysis_date <- as.Date("2006-12-31")
rfm_result <- rfm_table_order(rfm_data_orders, customer_id, order_date, revenue, analysis_date)
rfm_result
```

```{r rfm_table_order2, eval=TRUE, echo=FALSE}
analysis_date <- as.Date("2006-12-31")
rfm_result <- rfm_table_order(rfm_data_orders, customer_id, order_date, revenue, analysis_date)
rfm_result$rfm[1:10, ] %>%
  select(customer_id, recency_days, transaction_count, amount, rfm_score, recency_score, frequency_score, monetary_score, first_name, last_name, email) %>% 
  kable() %>%
  kable_styling()
```

## The six segments

The recommended scheme crosses the recency score with a combined frequency-monetary score, `fm = round((F + M) / 2)`.

Base R's `round()` rounds halves to even, so the result is deterministic; on this data 393 of the 995 customers sit exactly on a half.

The six rules cover all 25 R x FM cells exactly once, so every customer lands in exactly one segment and there are no `Others`.

| Segment | Rule | Action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Champions | R 4–5 and FM 4–5 | Reward them: early access, referrals; no discounts needed |
| Loyal | R 3 and FM 4–5, or R 4–5 and FM 3 | Cross-sell, loyalty perks, move them up to Champions |
| New / promising | R 4–5 and FM 1–2 | Onboarding and a second-purchase nudge |
| Needs attention | R 3 and FM 1–3 | A timely reminder and a light offer |
| At risk (high value) | R 1–2 and FM 3–5 | Win-back: personal outreach, the strongest offer |
| Lost / hibernating | R 1–2 and FM 1–2 | Low-cost reactivation, or suppress to save spend |

Build `fm` on the `rfm_table_order()` result and map each pair of scores to a segment with `case_when()`.

```{r six_segments}
six_levels <- c("Champions", "Loyal", "New / promising", "Needs attention",
                "At risk (high value)", "Lost / hibernating")

six_segments <- rfm_result$rfm %>%
  mutate(
    fm = round((frequency_score + monetary_score) / 2),
    segment = case_when(
      recency_score >= 4 & fm >= 4 ~ "Champions",
      (recency_score == 3 & fm >= 4) | (recency_score >= 4 & fm == 3) ~ "Loyal",
      recency_score >= 4 & fm <= 2 ~ "New / promising",
      recency_score == 3 & fm <= 3 ~ "Needs attention",
      recency_score <= 2 & fm >= 3 ~ "At risk (high value)",
      recency_score <= 2 & fm <= 2 ~ "Lost / hibernating"
    ),
    segment = factor(segment, levels = six_levels)
  )

six_segments %>%
  count(segment) %>%
  kable() %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
```

Summarise the segments to see customers, orders, revenue and average order value, plus the revenue share and how long ago each group last ordered.

```{r six_segment_summary}
six_summary <- six_segments %>%
  group_by(segment) %>%
  summarise(
    customers = n(),
    orders = sum(transaction_count),
    revenue = sum(amount),
    median_days = median(recency_days),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    pct_customers = round(100 * customers / sum(customers), 1),
    pct_revenue = round(100 * revenue / sum(revenue), 1),
    revenue_per_customer = round(revenue / customers, 2),
    aov = round(revenue / orders, 2)
  ) %>%
  select(segment, customers, orders, revenue, pct_customers, pct_revenue,
         revenue_per_customer, aov, median_days)

six_summary %>%
  kable(
    col.names = c("Segment", "Customers", "Orders", "Revenue", "% customers",
                  "% revenue", "Revenue per customer", "AOV",
                  "Median days since last order")
  ) %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE)
```

`rfm_segment_summary(six_segments)` accepts the same labelled frame and returns customers, orders, revenue and average order value if you do not need the extra measures.

What the store owner learns:

- **Champions** are 202 customers (20.3%) and 31.0% of revenue, 711.39 each, with a median last order 114 days ago (about four months). Reward them with early access and referrals; they do not need a discount.
- **Loyal** are 139 customers (14.0%) and 17.6% of revenue, 588.48 each, with a median last order 193 days ago (about six months). Cross-sell and give them a reason to move up to Champions.
- **New / promising** are 144 customers (14.5%) but only 9.0% of revenue; their average order is 83.34 and their median last order 119 days ago (about four months). Most have already ordered several times (median 4), so treat them as recent, lower-spend buyers: onboard them, then raise the basket size or frequency to move them towards Loyal.
- **Needs attention** are 112 customers (11.3%) and 7.7% of revenue, with an 82.69 average order and a median last order 236 days ago (about eight months). A timely reminder and a light offer is the right spend.
- **At risk (high value)** are 161 customers (16.2%) and 21.4% of revenue, the second-largest revenue block: 615.63 each and a 101.76 average order, the highest of the six. Their last order is a median 449 days old (about 15 months), so this is the win-back list to call first.
- **Lost / hibernating** are the largest group at 237 customers (23.8%) but only 13.3% of revenue, 260.47 each, with a median last order 515 days ago (about 17 months). Use low-cost reactivation, or suppress them to save spend.

Every segment is at least 11% of customers. Past value is concentrated in Champions, Loyal and At risk (588–711 per customer); the other three are between 260 and 322 per customer, so each row carries one clear action.

## Plot the revenue share

A store owner can see at a glance where the revenue sits.

```{r six_revenue_share, fig.align='center', fig.width=7, fig.height=4, fig.alt="Bar chart of share of revenue by segment: Champions 31.0%, Loyal 17.6%, New / promising 9.0%, Needs attention 7.7%, At risk (high value) 21.4%, Lost / hibernating 13.3%."}
ggplot(six_summary, aes(x = segment, y = pct_revenue)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#3b5bdb") +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(sprintf("%.1f", pct_revenue), "%")),
            vjust = -0.4, size = 3.2) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Share of revenue (%)",
    title = "Revenue share by segment"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 20, hjust = 1))
```

## Example 2: the standard segments

The classic ten segments are defined on the three separate score boxes, and `rfm_segment()` applies them in order with the first match winning. The ten rules overlap in 58 of the 125 R x F x M score cells, so list order matters: "Potential Loyalist" covers many high-frequency, high-monetary customers because it is listed second with a wide box (R 3–5, F 3–5, M 2–5). Ten cells match no rule at all; customers there become `Others` (none in this data). Each bound below is inclusive on both ends.

```{r segments, echo=FALSE}
segment <- c("Champions", "Potential Loyalist", "Loyal Customers", 
             "Promising", "New Customers", "Can't Lose Them", 
             "At Risk", "Need Attention", "About To Sleep", "Lost")
description <- c(
  "Bought recently, buy often and spend the most",
  "Recent customers, spent good amount, bought more than once",
  "Spend good money. Responsive to promotions",
  "Recent shoppers; the rule needs a monetary score of 3–5, so only large first baskets qualify",
  "Bought more recently, but not often",
  "Made big purchases and often, but long time ago",
  "Spent big money, purchased often but long time ago",
  "Above average recency, frequency & monetary values",
  "Below average recency, frequency & monetary values",
  "Bought a long time ago, average amount spent"
)
recency <-   c("5", "3 - 5", "2 - 4", "3 - 4", "4 - 5", "1 - 2", "1 - 2", "1 - 3", "2 - 3", "1 - 1")
frequency <- c("5", "3 - 5", "2 - 4", "1 - 3", "1 - 3", "3 - 4", "2 - 5", "3 - 5", "1 - 3", "1 - 5")
monetary <-  c("5", "2 - 5", "2 - 4", "3 - 5", "1 - 5", "4 - 5", "4 - 5", "3 - 5", "1 - 4", "1 - 5")
segments <- data.frame(
  Segment = segment, Description = description,
  R = recency, `F` = frequency, M = monetary
)

segments %>%
  kable() %>%
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, font_size = 12)
```

Assign the labels with those rules.

```{r criteria, echo=FALSE}
segment_names <- c("Champions", "Potential Loyalist", "Loyal Customers", 
                   "Promising", "New Customers", "Can't Lose Them", 
                   "At Risk", "Need Attention", "About To Sleep", "Lost")

recency_lower <-   c(5, 3, 2, 3, 4, 1, 1, 1, 2, 1)
recency_upper <-   c(5, 5, 4, 4, 5, 2, 2, 3, 3, 1)
frequency_lower <- c(5, 3, 2, 1, 1, 3, 2, 3, 1, 1)
frequency_upper <- c(5, 5, 4, 3, 3, 4, 5, 5, 3, 5)
monetary_lower <-  c(5, 2, 2, 3, 1, 4, 4, 3, 1, 1)
monetary_upper <-  c(5, 5, 4, 5, 5, 5, 5, 5, 4, 5)

segments <- rfm_segment(rfm_result, segment_names, recency_lower, recency_upper,
frequency_lower, frequency_upper, monetary_lower, monetary_upper)

segments %>%
  head(10) %>%
  kable() %>%
  kable_styling()
```

The ten rules claim all 995 customers; no customer falls through to `Others`.

Let us quickly summarise the segments to get an overview of the number of customers, orders and average order value in each of them.

#### Segment Summary

```{r segment_summary}
rfm_segment_summary(segments)
```

`rfm` package offers visualisation tools to validate the segments generated from the RFM score. Below are a few of them:

#### Segmentation Plot

```{r segment_plot, fig.align='center', fig.width=7, fig.height=7}
segments %>%
  rfm_segment_summary() %>%
  rfm_plot_segment()
```

#### Segment Summary Plot

```{r segment_sumamry_plot, fig.align='center', fig.width=7, fig.height=7}
segments %>%
  rfm_segment_summary() %>%
  rfm_plot_segment_summary()
```

#### Revenue Distribution

```{r revenue_dist_plot, fig.align='center', fig.width=7, fig.height=7}
segments %>%
  rfm_segment_summary() %>%
  rfm_plot_revenue_dist()
```
